items.title: Optional per-schema change-log tables for schema-per-tenant deployments (structural isolation without RLS)
items.body:
## Background

The change-spine change-log lives in a single shared table `core.tb_entity_change_log` for **all** deployments, regardless of tenancy mode. #443 (audit #437 F6) added Row-Level Security to it so a non-`BYPASSRLS` role is deny-by-default — defence-in-depth for a table that holds every tenant's before/after payloads. That fix is correct for **row-mode** tenancy (shared tables + WHERE-injection), where one shared change-log is the natural model.

But FraiseQL also supports **schema-per-tenant** tenancy (`[fraiseql.tenancy] mode = "schema"`): the adapter issues `SET search_path TO tenant_{key}, public` per request and `TenantExecutorFactory` provisions/drops a schema per tenant. For those deployments, a **per-schema change-log table** (`tenant_{key}.tb_entity_change_log`) would give tenant isolation *structurally* — search_path already scopes reads to the tenant's schema — with **no RLS, no `BYPASSRLS` requirement, and no silent-empty-pipeline footgun**. It's arguably the cleaner posture for the schema-isolation users who already accept per-tenant schemas.

This issue proposes making the change-log's location an **opt-in choice** so schema-per-tenant deployments can keep the change-log inside the tenant schema instead of the shared `core` schema.

## Proposed shape (opt-in)

A config toggle (e.g. `[changelog] location = "shared" | "per_tenant_schema"`, default `shared`) selecting where the change-log contract is installed:

- `shared` (today): `core.tb_entity_change_log` + the #443 RLS posture. Unchanged default.
- `per_tenant_schema`: the contract table, views, capture-trigger function, and per-table triggers are installed into each tenant schema; reads scope via search_path; no RLS needed for the table itself.

There is a useful existing seam: the GraphQL `entity_change_logs` query already qualifies its source with a configurable schema (`crates/fraiseql-core/src/schema/changelog.rs` — `with_sql_source(format!("{}.v_entity_change_log", cfg.schema))`), so the read side is partly parameterized already.

## The hard part — CDC fan-out (why this is a design discussion, not a toggle)

The reason the change-log is shared today is the **cross-tenant CDC fan-out**: the poller (`crates/fraiseql-observers/src/listener/change_log.rs`) and the three NATS bridges (`crates/fraiseql-observers/src/transport/{bridge,mysql_bridge,mssql_bridge}.rs`) read **one** ordered stream (`ORDER BY pk_entity_change_log`) across all tenants and fan out events. Per-schema tables break that single stream:

- Polling N per-tenant schemas does not scale and has no defined global ordering.
- A monotonic global cursor (`pk_entity_change_log` / `seq`) no longer exists across schemas.
- Subscription matching, dedup `(object_type, seq)`, and `nats_event_id` mark-published all assume one table.

So the open question is **how CDC consumers source events under per-schema tables** — candidates: a PG `PUBLICATION` across the per-tenant tables, logical replication, a per-tenant poller/stream, or an aggregating outbox. Each has real trade-offs. This needs design before implementation.

## Affected components

- Migrations `08_*`/`11_*`/`12_*` (contract table, capture-trigger fn, RLS) — installed per-schema instead of into `core`.
- `fraiseql generate capture-triggers` — emit triggers into the tenant schema.
- `TenantExecutorFactory` schema provisioning — install the change-log contract when a tenant schema is created.
- Poller + 3 NATS bridges — the fan-out sourcing question above.
- Server changelog HTTP handlers (`crates/fraiseql-server/src/observers/changelog_handlers/mod.rs`) + the `entity_change_logs` query.
- `fraiseql doctor` — the change-log RLS / contract-drift checks become per-schema.

## Out of scope / notes

- Default stays `shared` + RLS (#443). This is purely additive opt-in.
- Row-mode tenancy is unaffected (shared table is correct there).
- Not a security fix — F6 is already closed by #443. This is an isolation-model option for schema-per-tenant users who'd prefer structural isolation over RLS.

Refs #443, #437 (F6).

items.title: ISSUE-5481: CDC Debezium Connector isn't allowing to specify replication slot name
items.body:
Original Issue: apache/pulsar#5481 

---

I think that it's safe to say that Apache Pulsar has multi-tenancy as a first-class citizen. However, when using it with CDC PostgreSQL Debezium Connector we actually have a issue that isn't allowing to separate data from different tenants.

Most companies use a schema-per-tenant approach when it comes to multi-tenancy so it is desirable to have a source connector for each schema. However, when using a standard configuration for PostgreSQL CDC Source Connector it creates a replication slot with the name "debezium" on PostgreSQL database. If we try to specify "slot.name" property it simply replies with "IO Exception". 

**It would be desirable to allow to specify the pg_replication_slot's name (possibly with the tenant's name) and this could be fixed by allowing to use Debezium's "slot.name" property.**

items.title: Explore single-process multi-tenant SQLite runtime for shared-schema workloads
items.body:
## Summary

Explore a **shared-schema multi-tenant application runtime** where one server process/orchestrator multiplexes many physically isolated SQLite/libSQL databases, typically one DB per application tenant, while exposing a single Convex-like developer experience.

This is not a proposal to replace Norn's current per-tenant storage direction. Norn already benefits from tenant-isolated databases because organizations may have different ontology, configuration, extensions, placement, and lifecycle. The question here is whether the same underlying primitive becomes even more efficient for conventional SaaS where every customer runs essentially the same schema and application code.

## Core architecture

Instead of shared tables with `tenant_id` + RLS, or one heavyweight database server/process per tenant:

```
                  ONE NODE / PROCESS
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ API / query / function runtime           │
│                  │                       │
│          tenant-aware router             │
│                  │                       │
│      ┌───────────┼───────────┐           │
│      ▼           ▼           ▼           │
│    A.db        B.db        C.db           │
│   SQLite      SQLite      SQLite          │
│                                          │
│ shared runtime, schema, migrations,      │
│ authz, realtime, caches, telemetry       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

SQLite is in-process, so this is not N SQLite server processes. Maintain a bounded/LRU set of open handles for hot tenants; cold tenants remain durable state with essentially no dedicated compute or RAM.

At larger scale:

```
                    Global router
                         │
                tenant → placement
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ▼              ▼              ▼
        Node A          Node B          Node C
       many DBs        many DBs        many DBs
```

The tenant DB becomes the native shard, isolation, lifecycle, and mobility unit.

## Why this may be efficient for shared-schema SaaS

For something like a todo SaaS:

```
Todo App
schema v42
functions v17
indexes ...
      │
      ├── tenant A.db
      ├── tenant B.db
      ├── tenant C.db
      └── tenant D.db
```

Almost everything can be amortized.

**Shared per application/process**
- SQLite/libSQL engine
- function/runtime code
- schema definition
- generated query code / prepared-query templates
- migration definitions
- authorization engine
- realtime/sync machinery
- telemetry
- handle/cache management

**Per tenant**
- SQLite DB/state
- WAL/replication state
- routing/schema-version metadata
- working-set cache only while active

The hypothesis is that this can achieve very high density for huge numbers of small or mostly-idle tenants while retaining stronger physical isolation than shared-table tenancy.

## Isolation and AuthZ

Do not make RLS the application authorization abstraction.

```
request
→ authenticate
→ resolve application + tenant
→ authorize subject/action/resource/context
→ route to tenant DB
→ execute
```

Normal queries should not require `WHERE tenant_id = ?`: another tenant's rows simply do not exist in the selected database.

Within-tenant permissions remain an AuthZ/policy problem. DB-level mechanisms may still exist as defense in depth.

## Convex-like DX hypothesis

Investigate whether this substrate makes a Convex-like backend much easier without building a storage engine from scratch.

```ts
export const createTodo = mutation({
  args: { text: v.string() },
  handler: async (ctx, args) => {
    return ctx.db.insert("todos", {
      text: args.text,
      completed: false,
    });
  },
});
```

Internally:

```
request
→ identity
→ application
→ tenant
→ authz
→ placement/router
→ tenant SQLite/libSQL DB
→ transaction
```

Developer mental model: one application/database.

Physical model: potentially hundreds of thousands or millions of isolated SQLite DBs sharing one application definition.

## Realtime / Zero

Explore a Zero-style sync layer instead of reproducing Convex's reactive database internals from scratch:

```
client reactive query
        │
local materialized state
        │
      sync
        │
realtime gateway
        │
tenant change stream
        │
tenant.db
```

Tenant DBs are naturally independent synchronization domains.

Research:
- current Zero architecture and DB assumptions
- feasibility over SQLite/libSQL/Turso
- direct adoption vs adaptation vs borrowing protocol/query architecture
- SQLite/libSQL hooks/CDC/change capture
- dependency/invalidation granularity
- optimistic writes and offline operation
- keeping realtime gateways separate from DB compute so WebSockets do not pin tenant runtimes

## Scale to zero

Target lifecycle:

```
HOT
resident handle/runtime/cache
   ↓ idle
WARM
cached handle/placement
   ↓ idle
COLD
durable DB only
CPU ≈ 0
RAM ≈ 0
```

Activation:

```
request
→ route
→ acquire worker
→ open/attach DB
→ execute
→ eventually evict
```

The difficult part is not suspension itself but fast/correct activation: concurrent wakeups, write ownership, WAL/replication catch-up, migration state, cache reconstruction, subscriptions, and routing races.

## Shared schema + fleet migrations

One desired schema:

```
application desired_schema = v58
```

Independent convergence:

```
A.db v58 ✓
B.db v58 ✓
C.db v57 → migrate
D.db cold → potentially migrate on activation
```

Investigate eager vs lazy migration, compatibility windows, canaries, failure isolation, extremely stale cold DBs, schema-version routing, and whether prepared query/schema metadata can be shared across identically shaped DB handles.

## Hot tenant graduation

Application code should remain unchanged as physical placement changes:

```
cold tenant → shared node
active tenant → sticky/warm worker
hot tenant → dedicated worker/node
very large tenant → dedicated replication/resources
```

Explore live tenant movement, draining, replication/copy, router cutover, and useful libSQL/Turso primitives.

## Cross-tenant operations

Cross-tenant queries become fan-out/distributed operations. Treat this as an explicit tradeoff.

Prefer:

```
tenant OLTP DBs
      │
   CDC/events
      ▼
shared analytical plane / lake / OLAP / derived indexes
```

rather than compromising tenant OLTP isolation for global analytics.

## Relationship to Norn

Keep these motivations separate:

**Norn native tenant runtime**
```
organization
→ unique DB/runtime
→ potentially unique ontology/schema/config/extensions
```

Tenant is a genuine computational/data domain.

**Shared-schema application runtime**
```
application definition
→ identical schema/code
→ many isolated tenant DBs
```

Tenant is primarily an isolation/sharding/lifecycle/placement domain.

The latter may reuse Norn infrastructure for routing, placement, SQLite/libSQL lifecycle, backups, replication, migrations, AuthZ, observability, runtime scheduling, scale-to-zero, and realtime.

## Key research questions

- What existing systems implement **one process multiplexing many independent SQLite DBs**, not merely provisioning one remote DB service per tenant?
- How many SQLite/libSQL DBs can one process/node realistically manage?
- Practical open-handle/file-descriptor limits and optimal LRU strategy?
- Filesystem/object-storage metadata cost at 10k/100k/1m DBs?
- WAL and page-cache overhead per hot DB?
- Can prepared statements/query plans/schema metadata be amortized across identically shaped DBs?
- Best write-ownership model?
- Which libSQL/Turso replication components are reusable/embeddable?
- Can a tenant move between nodes with negligible downtime?
- Cold activation latency?
- Failure mode when one tenant exceeds SQLite's preferred write/concurrency envelope?
- Can Zero provide the realtime/client-sync layer?
- What Convex semantics still need to be implemented above SQLite?
- Which remaining pieces are database-engine work versus platform/runtime work?
- Economics vs shared Postgres + RLS, Neon-style serverless Postgres, D1, Turso Cloud database-per-tenant, and conventional sharding?

## Prototype / benchmark

Build a deliberately small benchmark before committing architecturally:

1. Single Rust process.
2. One common schema.
3. Generate 10k–100k small tenant SQLite/libSQL DBs.
4. Tenant-aware request router.
5. Bounded LRU DB-handle cache.
6. Mixed concurrent read/write workload with realistic hot/warm/cold distribution.
7. Measure cold-open latency, warm latency, throughput, RAM, FDs, disk/cache behavior, WAL overhead, and noisy-neighbor effects.
8. Apply one schema migration using eager and lazy fleet strategies.
9. Move a live tenant between two worker processes/nodes.
10. Prototype change capture + realtime subscription for a small todo app.
11. Compare where useful with shared SQLite/Postgres and hosted Turso/D1-style approaches.

## Success criteria

Interesting if evidence shows:
- idle tenant marginal CPU/RAM approaches zero;
- one node can economically host a very large DB fleet;
- activation latency is interactive;
- hot tenants can graduate without app changes;
- shared-schema fleet migration is tractable;
- realtime can be layered on without inventing a storage engine;
- physical tenancy materially simplifies application multitenancy;
- Convex-like DX is plausible while delegating transactions/query planning/storage to SQLite/libSQL.

## Non-goals

- Do not replace Norn's existing tenant-storage direction based on this exploration.
- Do not build a SQL parser, planner, B-tree, WAL, or transactional engine unless evidence requires it.
- Do not assume Turso Cloud is required; distinguish hosted Turso from reusable libSQL/Turso technology.
- Do not assume Zero is the realtime answer until current compatibility is verified.
- Do not optimize for cross-tenant OLTP transactions.

**Deliverable:** research plus a benchmarkable prototype design, not a production implementation.

items.title: Postgres CDC: error when syncing inherited tables where child has different schema than parent
items.body:
### Summary
When running Postgres CDC with `PEERDB_POSTGRES_CDC_HANDLE_INHERITANCE_FOR_NON_PARTITIONED_TABLES` enabled and the source uses old-style `INHERITS` tables (not declarative partitioning), child tables with **extra columns** beyond the parent's schema cause tuple decoding failures or cross-child data corruption.

Unlike partitioned tables where all partitions share an identical column layout, `INHERITS` children can add their own columns (e.g. `stripe_payment` inherits 18 columns from `payment` and adds `fk_stripe_payment` and `stripe_account_id`). The WAL emits tuples using the child's column layout, but PeerDB was decoding them using the wrong RelationMessage.

### Root cause
When a child table's `RelationMessage` arrived in the WAL stream, `processMessage` mutated `msg.RelationID` from the child's ID to the parent's:
```go
msg.RelationID, err = p.checkIfUnknownTableInherits(ctx, msg.RelationID)
```
This caused `processRelationMessage` to store the child's RelationMessage under the **parent's** relation ID:
```go
p.relationMessageMapping[currRel.RelationID] = currRel  // stored under parent's ID
```
Then in `processInsertMessage` / `processUpdateMessage` / `processDeleteMessage`, the RelationMessage was looked up using the parent's ID:
```go
rel, ok := p.relationMessageMapping[relID]  // relID = parent's ID
```
This had two consequences:
1. **Cross-child contamination**: multiple children's RelationMessages overwrote each other under the same parent key — whichever child sent last determined the column layout used for all children.
2. **Positional mismatch**: a child with extra columns (e.g. 20 columns) had its tuple decoded using a RelationMessage from a different child or the parent (e.g. 18 columns), causing columns to be decoded with the wrong types.

### Fix
- Stop mutating `msg.RelationID` in the `RelationMessage` handler. Store each child's RelationMessage under its **own** relation ID.
- In `processInsertMessage` / `processUpdateMessage` / `processDeleteMessage`, use the child's actual relation ID (`actualRelID`) for RelationMessage lookup (correct tuple decoding), and the parent's relation ID (`relID`) only for table name and destination routing.
- In `processRelationMessage`, resolve to the parent via `getParentRelIDIfPartitioned` for name/schema lookups, but leave `currRel.RelationID` untouched for storage.

items.body:
## Situation

The platform is greenfield. There is no single place where a field is declared to be PHI, PII, sensitive, operational or analytical, and no machine-readable mapping from those classifications to the controls that must apply (encryption, access rule, retention period, export eligibility, analytics eligibility). Today every service would decide independently whether a column may leave the operational database, appear in a log line, be copied to the OLAP warehouse, or be included in a subject-access export. That is exactly how PHI leaks into dashboards and log aggregators.

This affects everyone downstream: the DPO, who cannot answer "where does this data live and what protects it" without reading source code; the compliance team, who must produce evidence for NABH audits and for tenant security questionnaires; and every backend engineer, who currently has no authoritative answer to "may I put this field in an event payload?".

MediCore, MediConnect, LabConnect and PharmaConnect all handle clinical data, but the concrete legal instrument varies by tenant and country — DPDP Act 2023 for India (issue #57), HIPAA for a future US deployment (#58), GDPR for EU (#59). The controls those regimes demand overlap heavily: classify data, encrypt it, restrict access on a need-to-know basis, log access tamper-evidently, retain it for a defined period, delete it on a defined trigger, and notify on breach. This issue builds that shared control baseline once, so the regime-specific issues become configuration and evidence rather than three parallel implementations.

Without it, #57, #58 and #59 each reimplement classification and each drifts.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** Data Protection Officer and as a platform engineer
**I want** every persisted field classified in a machine-readable registry that drives encryption, access, logging, retention and export controls
**So that** privacy obligations are enforced by the platform rather than by developer memory, and evidence can be produced on demand.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A data classification registry: every table and column in the operational schema tagged `phi`, `pii`, `sensitive`, `operational` or `analytical`, with a purpose and a lawful-basis hint.
* A control matrix mapping each classification to required controls: encryption at rest, whether the field may appear in a NATS JetStream event payload, whether it may be replicated to OLAP, log-redaction behaviour, default retention class.
* A Go struct-tag convention (`privacy:"phi,retention=clinical_10y"`) plus a CI check that fails the build if a GORM model has an untagged field, or if a tagged PHI field is serialised into an event schema not on the allow-list.
* Automatic redaction in the shared logging/OpenTelemetry middleware driven by the registry — PHI and sensitive fields are hashed or dropped before a log or span attribute is emitted.
* A field-level encryption helper for the `sensitive` class (Aadhaar-derived tokens, government identifiers) using envelope encryption with per-tenant data keys.
* An `AdminConnect` read-only compliance view rendering the registry: field, classification, stores it lands in, retention class, last reviewed.
* Registry export as a signed artefact for use as audit evidence and to seed the GDPR Article 30 record (#59).

**Out of scope**

* DPDP notice, grievance and breach-reporting workflow — owned by #57.
* HIPAA BAA register and minimum-necessary role mapping — owned by #58.
* GDPR lawful-basis register, DPIA and transfer mechanism — owned by #59.
* Consent capture and artefact lifecycle — owned by #60; this issue only records which classifications are consent-gated.
* Execution of deletion and retention jobs — owned by #63; this issue defines the retention classes those jobs consume.

---

## Recommended Solution

Implement the registry as first-class data in PostgreSQL 16, not as a spreadsheet, so it can be queried by services and by CI.

```sql
CREATE TABLE data_classification (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  schema_name     text NOT NULL,
  table_name      text NOT NULL,
  column_name     text NOT NULL,
  classification  text NOT NULL
    CHECK (classification IN ('phi','pii','sensitive','operational','analytical')),
  purpose         text NOT NULL,
  retention_class text NOT NULL REFERENCES retention_class(code),
  event_emittable boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  olap_eligible   boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  log_action      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'drop'
    CHECK (log_action IN ('drop','hash','mask_last4','allow')),
  reviewed_by     uuid, reviewed_at timestamptz,
  UNIQUE (schema_name, table_name, column_name)
);

CREATE TABLE retention_class (
  code text PRIMARY KEY,          -- clinical_10y, billing_8y, session_90d, ephemeral_24h
  min_retention interval NOT NULL,
  max_retention interval,
  legal_basis   text NOT NULL,
  deletable_on_request boolean NOT NULL
);
```

The registry is a control-plane table (feature/config data, not PHI), so it is not tenant-scoped; the country profile can override `retention_class` per country via a `retention_class_override(country_code, code, min_retention)` table, satisfying the country-profile rule rather than branching on `country == "IN"`.

Enforcement runs at three points:

1. **Build time.** A `go vet`-style analyser walks all GORM models, reconciles struct fields against `data_classification`, and fails CI on any unclassified field or on a PHI field referenced by an event schema whose subject is not in the allow-list. This is the single most valuable control because it prevents drift.
2. **Runtime, on emission.** The shared logging and OTel exporters consult a registry snapshot cached in Redis (`privacy:registry:v{n}`, refreshed on `DataClassificationChanged`) and apply `log_action` before the record leaves the process. Span attributes go through the same filter — traces are a common PHI leak path.
3. **Runtime, on replication.** The OLAP change-data-capture sink drops any column where `olap_eligible = false`, so the analytics warehouse cannot receive identifiable PHI by accident. This is the mechanical enforcement of the OLTP/OLAP separation rule.

Field-level encryption for `sensitive` uses envelope encryption: a per-tenant data encryption key wrapped by a KMS key, with the wrapped key stored in `tenant_crypto_key`. Keeping keys per tenant makes crypto-shredding a viable erasure mechanism for #63 and is a hard dependency for it — land this issue first.

API surface (AdminConnect, DPO role only):

```
GET  /api/v1/privacy/classifications?table=&classification=
GET  /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}
PUT  /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}      # requires dual approval
GET  /api/v1/privacy/retention-classes
POST /api/v1/privacy/registry/export           # signed evidence bundle
GET  /api/v1/privacy/coverage                  # % of columns classified
```

Events published: `DataClassificationChanged` (invalidates the Redis snapshot and the CDC column filter) and `PrivacyRegistryExported` (audit trail).

OpenFGA model — the registry is a governance object, not clinical data, so relations are narrow:

```
type privacy_registry
  relations
    define viewer: [user, role#member]
    define editor: [role#member]
    define approver: [role#member]   # dual control: editor != approver
```

`PUT` requires a second principal holding `approver` before the change takes effect; the change is staged in `data_classification_pending` until approved. Reclassifying a field from `phi` to `operational` is the obvious attack path — dual control plus a permanent audit record is the mitigation.

Sequencing: this issue has no upstream dependency and blocks #57, #58, #59 and #63. Consent (#60) can proceed in parallel.

Principal risks. First, the CI analyser producing so much noise that teams disable it — mitigate by seeding the registry from the existing schema with an explicit `unclassified` backlog and enforcing the gate only on new and changed models for the first two sprints. Second, the Redis snapshot going stale and PHI reaching logs — mitigate with a version counter checked on every process start and a fail-closed default (`log_action = 'drop'`) when the snapshot is unavailable. Third, performance of per-field redaction in hot paths — the filter is a precomputed field-index map, not reflection, and is benchmarked as part of the acceptance threshold.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a GORM model field classified as `phi` with `log_action = 'drop'`
**When** a service logs a struct containing that field and emits an OTel span with it as an attribute
**Then** neither the log record nor the exported span contains the value, the field is absent rather than empty-stringed, and the surrounding diagnostic context is preserved.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** the Redis registry snapshot is unavailable and no local cache is warm
**When** a service attempts to emit a log line or replicate a row to OLAP
**Then** the platform fails closed — all non-`operational` fields are dropped, a `privacy_registry_unavailable` metric is incremented, and the OLAP sink pauses rather than replicating unfiltered rows.

### Edge Cases

* A developer adds a new column to a GORM model without a `privacy` tag — CI fails with the exact file, struct and field name.
* A JSONB column (for example a FHIR `Observation` payload) holds mixed classifications — the registry supports JSON-path level entries and the redactor walks them.
* A field is reclassified from `sensitive` to `pii` — the pending change is visible to the editor but has no runtime effect until an approver who is not the editor confirms it.
* An engineer with `viewer` but not `editor` calls `PUT /api/v1/privacy/classifications/{id}` — 403, and the attempt is written to the tamper-evident audit log.
* A tenant on the schema-per-tenant premium tier — the registry resolves classification by logical table name, not physical schema, so all tenant schemas are covered by one entry.
* Retention class override exists for a country profile but the base class does not — write is rejected by the foreign key rather than silently defaulting.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* Expected user or system outcome: every persisted column carries a classification, and redaction, OLAP eligibility and retention are derived from it automatically.
* Expected business or operational outcome: the DPO can answer a tenant security questionnaire or an accreditation query from the registry export without engineering involvement.
* Success metric or validation method: 100% of columns in the operational schema classified with zero `unclassified` entries at merge; zero PHI-classified values found by the log-scanner probe across a 7-day sample of production logs and traces; redaction adds no more than 0.4 ms to p95 request latency measured against the MediCore OPD endpoint.
* Monitoring period, where applicable: 30 days post-deployment, tracking `privacy_registry_unavailable` and the weekly log-scanner probe result.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — full WCAG coverage.
**Reason:** The only interface is a read-only DPO-facing registry table in AdminConnect built from shared design-system components; the substance of this issue is backend enforcement.
**Alternative validation:** The registry view is built from already-audited design-system table and filter components, and is checked with axe for the table, filter and export controls only.
**Residual risk:** Low. The audience is a small internal role and no clinical decision depends on this view.
**Approved by:** Compliance Team lead.

items.body:
🦫🎙️   dispatch to foreman
```
💧 task enqueued
   ├─ priority = ?
   ├─ yieldage = ?
   └─ leverage = ?
```
**title**
a tenant repo has no brief for db-major-cutover readiness
**description**
# 🌙 dream: a tenant repo's db-major-cutover readiness has no brief

| | |
|---|---|
| kind | reseed |
| owner | `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ehmpathy` — `role=mechanic`, a new `practices/data.cutover/` cluster |
| caught | 2026-09-28 |
| evidence | `ahbode/svc-chat` `.behavior/v2026_09_28.fix-pg-upgrade/` — the whole vision stage |

## .the cue that fired

a route was pointed at *"upgrade svc-chat postgres off extended support"*. the first measurement
struck the premise: `grep engine_version` in svc-chat returns **0 hits**. the engine is declared
once, in another repo, for a cluster ~20 logical databases across 22 repos share.

⇒ the route re-derived, from scratch, the whole shape of **what a dependent service owes a major
version cutover it does not control**. every one of the lessons below cost a measurement, and not
one of them is svc-chat-specific.

## .the gap, precisely

there is no brief anywhere in the org on db major cutovers. so the next tenant repo that meets
this — and there are ~21 more on this one cluster — pays the same discovery again, and will
likely pay it worse, because three of the six lessons below are **counter-intuitive** and the
default belief is the wrong one.

### the six, each measured rather than reasoned

**1. the owner/tenant split is the reframe, and it must come first.**
a shared cluster means the repo that **depends** on the engine is not the repo that **declares**
it. a tenant's deliverable is therefore **readiness** — audit, conform, prove — plus one runnable
ask handed up. that is work a tenant can finish; *"do the upgrade"* is not.
⇒ the tell that you are a tenant: `grep engine_version` returns **no hit** in your own repo.

**2. 🔴 engine skew is bidirectional, and most preflights check one direction.**
a CI job that reaches both a pinned local testdb and a live cluster can read green against the
wrong engine. it arrives two ways:
- you bump the local pin **ahead** of the cluster — the obvious one
- the cluster **falls back under** a pin that already moved — a peer tenant's upgrade fails its
  post-checks and the shared cluster is restored

⇒ the second arrives **by no act of your own**, and lands you in the identical end state. an
invariant stated against one path holds against one path.

**3. 🔴 one halt shape, two fix lines.**
a preflight that detects *"the majors differ"* must also know **why** they differ, because the
remedy inverts. *"flip the cluster first"* is correct when the flip has not run — and in the
fallback world that advice names **the act that just failed**, so an operator who follows it
re-attempts an upgrade a peer's post-checks already rejected.

**4. the seam taxonomy — and the three that do not fire are worth as much as the three that do.**

| fires | does not fire |
|---|---|
| extensions carry forward at their **old** version — `ALTER EXTENSION … UPDATE` is owed | the PG15 public-schema revoke — **carved out** for upgrades |
| planner statistics **reset** — a full `ANALYZE` is owed | scram **on the flip** — extant md5 hashes are preserved |
| a password **write after** the flip stores a scram hash — a **sequence**, not the flip | a modern `pg` driver — it ships SASL |

⇒ 🔴 **the scram row is the one everybody gets wrong.** the widely-held belief is that a pg
major break auth. it does not; the break is deferred to the next password **rotation**, which
can be months later and will look unrelated. a readiness report that lists a hazard which
provably does not fire makes a reader over-price the work — which is its own defect.

⇒ **the extension + `ANALYZE` debt is per database, so each tenant owns its own list.** the
cluster flip is one act; its after-steps are N — one per logical database, each with a different
extension set (chatdb: `uuid-ossp`, `pgcrypto`; jobsdb adds `cube`, `earthdistance`). a
cluster-level runbook that lists one set misses the rest. svc-chat paved the per-tenant form:
`provision/schema/sql/upgrade/after_major_upgrade.sql`, its list held equal to `.extensions.sql`
by a test.

**5. 🔴 a peer tenant's replication slot blocks your in-place upgrade.**
`pg_upgrade` refuses to run while any logical replication slot exists. on a shared cluster the
slot is often held by a database you do not own — here, three peer DMS `full-load-and-cdc` tasks,
where svc-chat itself holds none. ⇒ your readiness can be complete and the upgrade still barred,
by a tenant you cannot reach.

**6. the unbounded connection is the failure mode a cutover actually produces.**
a cluster mid-cutover **accepts the socket and never answers**. with no `connectionTimeoutMillis`
and no `query_timeout`, a lambda burns its full duration per invocation rather than a fast fail.
⇒ this is the single cheapest pre-cutover repair, it is worth doing whether or not the cutover
ever happens, and it is a practice-level defect rather than a per-repo one (see the paired dream).

**and the presupposition under all of it:** invariants of the form *"no migration / no deploy
inside the window"* each presuppose the tenant can **detect** the window. usually it cannot — the
flip is taken in another repo and another account. a **probe** (read the live engine version,
halt on a change) is the cheap repair; *"a human remembers"* is the honest status quo, and it is
worth saying aloud rather than to imply an automatic gate.

## .the shape of the fix

a `practices/data.cutover/` cluster under `ehmpathy/role=mechanic`:

| brief | carries |
|---|---|
| `define.tenant-vs-owner-of-a-shared-cluster` | lesson 1 — the reframe, and the `grep` tell |
| `rule.require.bidirectional-engine-skew-check` | lessons 2 + 3 — both arrival paths, and the two fix lines |
| `ref.pg-major-cutover-seams` | lesson 4 — the fires/does-not-fire table, each row with its citation |
| `rule.require.bounded-db-timeouts` | lesson 6 |
| `rule.require.detectability-before-a-window-invariant` | the presupposition |

🟡 **the fires/does-not-fire table is the highest-value single artifact**, because it is the one
that stops work rather than starts it — three hazards struck is three phases nobody plans.

## .why it is not done in this round

the briefs belong to `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ehmpathy`, not here. a tree adopts only what is
scoped to itself — so this is a **reseed**, and `.dream/` is the local queue: caught is not
dispatched.

⚠️ **an alternative home is `ehmpathy/rhachet-roles-ghlitch` `role=deployer`**, which already owns
`provision.database` and the `sql-schema-control` lessons. the case for `mechanic` is that five of
the six lessons are about **code and CI** rather than about a deploy; the case for `deployer` is
lesson 5 and the window. ⇒ a real fork, and it is the adopter's call rather than this route's.

items.body:
## Problem Statement

Finance and internal-control teams running Odoo cannot tell, day to day, whether their
Procure-to-Pay process is actually being followed. Approvals get skipped, purchase
orders get split to dodge thresholds, the same invoice gets paid twice, a vendor's bank
account is changed right before a payment — and they only discover it (if ever) during a
once-a-year external audit, long after the money is gone. Reconstructing what happened
means digging through hundreds of Odoo log lines by hand, and the ERP's own history can
be altered by the very insider under suspicion. They are blind between audits, and the
evidence they do have is not defensible.

## Solution

Bedrock is an AI Process Compliance Auditor that plugs into Odoo (read-only) and
continuously audits the Procure-to-Pay process. It reconstructs each PO's actual journey,
checks it against the expected Process and a library of deterministic Controls, and flags
behavioral outliers statistically. Every finding opens a Case bundling tamper-evident
Hard Evidence (kept in an independent ledger *outside* Odoo) with a plain-language AI
Narrative that explains it in seconds. Urgent, high-precision findings fire an Alert so a
human (or the customer's own ERP automation) can act before money moves; everything else
waits quietly in a Triage Queue. When a Case is closed, the Auditor attests to it and
Bedrock produces an immutable, exportable Audit Report — defensible proof that controls
are working. The AI is the Investigator; the human Auditor is always the Judge.

## User Stories

**Onboarding & connection**
1. As an Admin, I want to connect Bedrock to my Odoo instance with a read-only API key, so that I can start auditing without granting any write access to my ERP.
2. As an Admin, I want Bedrock to refuse to operate with anything more than read-only Odoo credentials, so that even a Bedrock compromise cannot alter my ERP.
3. As an Admin, I want Bedrock to backfill 6–12 months of my Odoo history on first connection, so that anomaly detection and conformance work from day one instead of after weeks of accumulation.
4. As an Admin, I want each Organization's data isolated in its own database schema, so that I can assure my CFO our financial evidence is not commingled with other customers.
5. As an Admin, I want to optionally install a thin Odoo automation/webhook, so that high-risk events reach Bedrock in near-real-time; and I want everything to still work (in batch) if I don't.

**Ingestion**
6. As an Auditor, I want Bedrock to poll my Odoo via its API on a schedule, so that bulk reconciliation Controls run without any customer-side install.
7. As an Auditor, I want hot events (vendor bank-account change, payment about to post, PO state change) pushed in near-real-time where my Odoo supports it, so that an Alert can beat the irreversible step.
8. As an Auditor, I want ingestion to degrade gracefully when push is unavailable, so that I still get detective coverage in batch.

**Process & conformance**
9. As an Auditor, I want Bedrock to reconstruct each PO's actual journey into a Process Instance, so that I can see how the real flow compares to how it's supposed to go.
10. As an Auditor, I want each Process Instance checked against the expected P2P Process (PR → PO → approval → Goods Receipt → Vendor Bill → 3-way match → Payment), so that skipped, out-of-order, or shortcut steps are caught as Conformance Deviations.
11. As an Auditor, I want a Conformance Deviation raised when a Goods Receipt is posted after payment, or an approval step is missing entirely, so that flow violations (not just record-level ones) are detected.

**Controls (deterministic rules)**
12. As an Auditor, I want a library of pre-built P2P Control Templates, so that I can switch on industry-standard checks without writing logic.
13. As an Auditor, I want to parameterize each Control (approval thresholds, who the CFO is, currency tolerances, exempt vendors), so that the checks match my company's actual SOP.
14. As an Auditor, I want a Rule Violation when a PO over my threshold lacks the required approval, so that authorization breaches are caught deterministically and explainably.
15. As an Auditor, I want split-PO detection, so that orders broken into pieces to dodge an approval threshold are flagged.
16. As an Auditor, I want duplicate-invoice and duplicate-vendor detection, so that double payments and fraudulent vendor clones are caught.
17. As an Auditor, I want 3-way-match checks across PO, Goods Receipt, and Vendor Bill, so that quantity/price mismatches surface before payment.
18. As an Auditor, I want every Violation to state exactly which Control it breached and why, so that I can stand behind the finding without re-deriving it.

**Anomaly detection (statistical)**
19. As an Auditor, I want behavioral outliers scored against a learned Baseline (timing, amount, frequency), so that suspicious patterns no fixed rule anticipated still surface.
20. As an Auditor, I want an Anomaly to be clearly a *candidate for review* with an Anomaly Score, never a verdict, so that I'm not misled into treating suspicion as fact.
21. As an Auditor, I want an Anomaly like "vendor bank account changed, then paid, within a window shorter than 99.8% of normal," so that classic fraud patterns are caught even outside the deterministic rules.

**Cases, evidence & narrative**
22. As an Auditor, I want every finding (Violation, Conformance Deviation, or Anomaly) to open a Case, so that nothing detected is ever silently dropped.
23. As an Auditor, I want each Case to bundle Hard Evidence (transaction id, IP, timestamps, before/after diff, modification history), so that I have the verdict-bearing facts I can sign on.
24. As an Auditor, I want Hard Evidence stored in an independent, append-only ledger outside Odoo, so that an insider who can rewrite Odoo's history cannot touch my evidence.
25. As an Auditor, I want a plain-language AI Narrative on each Case, so that I understand the story in ~30 seconds instead of reading hundreds of log lines.
26. As an Auditor, I want the AI Narrative kept clearly separate from and subordinate to the Hard Evidence, so that I always sign on facts, never on machine-generated prose.
27. As an Auditor, I want before/after diffs reconstructed from Odoo's own field-tracking when push isn't available, so that I still get change history without catching the change live.

**Alerts & noise control**
28. As an Auditor, I want only findings that clear a promotion gate (high Severity or high Anomaly Score, above the Materiality Floor, not suppressed, mature Baseline) to fire an Alert, so that Alerts stay rare and almost always real.
29. As an Auditor, I want everything else to land quietly in a Triage Queue with a periodic digest, so that I catch everything without being interrupted constantly.
30. As an Auditor, I want Alerts delivered via Slack / Telegram / SMS / webhook / API, so that they reach me (or my systems) on whatever channel I rely on.
31. As an Auditor, I want a noisy Control auto-demoted to Case-only when its Alert precision falls below target, so that one bad rule can't train me to ignore all Alerts.
32. As an Auditor, I want to mark a known-good pattern as a Suppression Rule, so that expected behavior stops generating Alerts.
33. As an Auditor, I want findings sharing the same vendor/rule/root-cause grouped into one Case, so that I don't drown in fifty Alerts for one underlying issue.
34. As the customer's ERP automation (Actuator), I want to receive a structured Alert webhook, so that I can freeze the order on my side — Bedrock never writes to Odoo itself.

**Case lifecycle, attestation & audit report**
35. As an Auditor, I want to work a Case through a clear lifecycle (open → triaged → investigating → confirmed | dismissed | accepted_risk → closed → exported), so that its status is unambiguous.
36. As an Auditor, I want to record a reason when I dismiss a Case, so that the false positive feeds Suppression Rules and self-tuning.
37. As an Auditor, I want to attest to a closed Case (identity-bound internal approval), so that there is a human decision of record — explicitly an Attestation, not a legal digital signature.
38. As an Auditor, I want to export an immutable Audit Report (Hard Evidence + my Attestation + timestamp, bound by a tamper-evidence hash), so that I have defensible proof for external auditors and regulators.
39. As an Auditor, I want the evidence ledger hash-chained and its head anchored outside Bedrock (periodic email to us + RFC-3161 timestamp), so that tampering is evident even against a Bedrock admin.
40. As a CFO/Controller, I want a Control Coverage view of which Controls are active and passing, so that I have ongoing assurance controls are working, not just an absence of alerts.

**Conversational access (MCP)**
41. As an Auditor, I want to query my compliance state from my AI assistant (Claude/ChatGPT) over a read-only MCP connection, so that I can ask "show me all split-PO Cases this quarter" or "summarize vendor X's risk" conversationally.
42. As an Admin, I want the MCP surface to be strictly read-only, so that connecting an AI assistant can never change a Case or touch Odoo.

## Implementation Decisions

- **New Ash domain `Bedrock.Compliance`**, added to `ash_domains`, alongside the existing `Bedrock.Accounts`. Core resources: `Organization`, `Connection`, `Control` (with `ControlTemplate` parameterization), `Process` (the expected model) / `ProcessInstance`, `Case`, finding records (`Violation`, `ConformanceDeviation`, `Anomaly`), `HardEvidence` entries, `AINarrative`, `Alert`, `SuppressionRule`, `AuditReport`. Names follow CONTEXT.md exactly.
- **Single ingestion seam.** Both the Oban poller and the inbound webhook controller funnel into one domain action (e.g. `ingest_events`) that takes a `Connection` and a batch of normalized Odoo records. The whole detection pipeline hangs off this action: normalize → **upsert to the Event History** → reconstruct `ProcessInstance` → evaluate Controls (Rule + Conformance) and statistical Anomaly scoring **over a replayed per-entity window (cross-batch)** → open `Case` → capture `HardEvidence` → run the Alert promotion gate. This is the highest seam and the one place tests drive the system.
- **Cross-batch correlation via a persisted Event History** (ADR-0011): under the poller one P2P process is naturally split across many Ingest Batches, so the seam upserts every normalized `Event` into a tenant-scoped **Event History** (pinning the field contract — `Money` / `Decimal`, evaluated per-currency — and a *semantic* dedup key) and **replays** a bounded per-detector window, so detection spans batches while detectors stay pure (ADR-0006). Findings are idempotent (an Episode-grained `finding_key`; re-ingestion opens no duplicate `Case`); conformance is monotonic-safe (omissions raised only at a *terminal* Process state, never retracted). This substrate is a **prerequisite of the real Odoo poller** and ships before it (#24 → #25, resolving #20–#23).
- **Three-layer detection** (CONTEXT.md / ADR-0004, ADR-0006): Layer 1 Deterministic Engine (Ash-evaluated Controls + conformance against the state-machine `Process`); Layer 2 Anomaly Engine as *lightweight statistics* (percentile / z-score on timing, amount, frequency) bootstrapped by onboarding backfill — **not** Isolation Forest/Autoencoders in v1; Layer 3 Context Weaver (LLM via `ash_ai` + RAG) producing the `AINarrative` only — never a verdict.
- **Read-only posture, alert-and-actuate** (ADR-0001, ADR-0002): Bedrock never writes to Odoo. Preventive value comes only from emitting an `Alert`; any freeze/write is performed by a customer-side Actuator (human or the customer's own ERP automation).
- **Hybrid ingestion** (ADR-0003): API polling via Oban is the universal floor; a thin Odoo Automated Action/webhook is an optional accelerator for hot events. CDC is out of scope.
- **Independent, tamper-evident Evidence Ledger** (ADR-0005, ADR-0009): append-only, encrypted (`ash_events` + `ash_paper_trail` + `ash_cloak`). Closed Cases are serialized to canonical JSON, SHA-256 hashed, **hash-chained**, and the chain head **externally anchored** (customer email + RFC-3161 timestamp). v1 ships internal **Attestation**, not a public-CA Digital Signature.
- **Case lifecycle** as an `ash_state_machine` (ADR-0008):
  `open → triaged → investigating → (confirmed | dismissed | accepted_risk) → closed → exported`; `dismissed` carries a reason that feeds Suppression Rules and self-tuning.
- **Alert promotion gate** (ADR-0010), conceptually:
  `promote_to_alert? = (severity >= :critical or anomaly_score >= :high) and money_at_risk >= materiality_floor and not suppressed? and baseline_mature?`
  Per-Control Alert precision is tracked; below target → auto-demote to Case-only. Default channels: every finding → `Case` in the Triage Queue (recall); only gated findings → `Alert` (precision).
- **Schema-per-tenant** (ADR-0007): Ash `:context` multitenancy keyed on `Organization`; each `Connection` stores a dedicated read-only Odoo credential encrypted via `ash_cloak`.
- **Outbound adapter ports** (behaviours, swapped via app config): an **Odoo client** port (poll/fetch) and an **Alert delivery** port (Slack/Telegram/SMS/webhook). `Alert` is persisted as an Ash resource; delivery is a side effect behind the port.
- **Read-only MCP server** reuses the existing OAuth 2.1 server (`scope: mcp`, DCR) to expose Cases/findings/evidence/narrative/coverage for conversational query. No write/triage over MCP in v1.

## Testing Decisions

- **A good test asserts external behavior, not implementation.** It drives the system through the `Bedrock.Compliance` domain code interface (call an action with inputs) and asserts on resulting domain state (which Cases/findings/evidence/alerts now exist, and their shape). It must not assert on private functions, intermediate structs, or module internals, so that the detection pipeline can be refactored freely.
- **One seam.** Tests `use Bedrock.DataCase`, set the tenant context (Ash `:context`), create an `Organization` + `Connection` via actions, feed canned Odoo records through the single `ingest_events` action, then assert: the right finding type opened the right `Case`; `HardEvidence` was captured; the Alert promotion gate fired (or didn't) per the inputs; the Audit Report export is immutable and hash-chained.
- **Outbound ports are stubbed, not asserted through.** The Odoo client is bypassed by calling `ingest_events` with fixtures directly; the Alert delivery port uses a recording test adapter, and assertions are made on the persisted `Alert` resource rather than real delivery.
- **Modules tested:** the `Bedrock.Compliance` domain actions — ingestion, Control/conformance evaluation, anomaly scoring (deterministic given fixed inputs/seeded baseline), Case lifecycle transitions, Alert promotion + suppression + self-tuning demotion, and Audit Report export/hash-chain integrity.
- **Prior art:** `Bedrock.DataCase` (Ecto SQL sandbox; supports `async: true`) is the existing data-layer test template — mirror it. The repo currently has only web controller tests (`test/bedrock_web/controllers/`); these new tests are the first domain-level suite and should follow standard Ash action-testing patterns against `DataCase`.
- **Determinism:** anomaly tests seed a fixed Baseline (via backfill fixtures) so percentile/z-score outcomes are reproducible; hash-chain tests assert that altering any committed Case record breaks chain verification.

## Out of Scope

Everything in `docs/ROADMAP.md`, specifically:
- **Preventive enforcement / write-back** into Odoo (blocking, freezing). Bedrock stays read-only; any write is the customer-side Actuator's.
- **Heavy ML** for Layer 2 (Isolation Forest, Autoencoders, embeddings) — v1 is statistical only.
- **CDC / logical replication** ingestion — v1 is poll + optional webhook.
- **NL Control authoring** — v1 ships parameterized Control Templates only.
- **MCP write/triage actions** — v1 MCP is read-only.
- **General process-mining platform** with customer-authored Process models — v1 has one pre-built P2P Process.
- **Other ERPs** (SAP, NetSuite, Dynamics, Vietnamese local) and **other processes** (O2C, standalone SoD).
- **Public-CA Digital Signature (chữ ký số)** of Audit Reports — deferred Enterprise add-on; v1 is internal Attestation + tamper-evidence.
- **Data-residency / multi-region** options.
- **Pricing/packaging.**

## Further Notes

- Vocabulary and rationale live in `CONTEXT.md` (glossary) and `docs/adr/0001`–`0011` (ADR-0011 = cross-batch correlation). `CONTEXT.md` now also defines `Event`, `Event History`, `Ingest Batch`, and `Episode`. Use the glossary terms exactly; do not drift to synonyms it marks `_Avoid_`.
- **Honesty constraint (ADR-0009):** never market or describe the ledger as "tamper-proof" — the supported claim is "tamper-evident (defends against a privileged insider, Tier B)." Court-grade non-repudiation requires the deferred CA add-on (Tier C).
- **Precision over volume (ADR-0010):** the product is judged on Alert precision, not Alert count. Fewer, truer Alerts is the explicit design goal — alert fatigue is treated as an existential product risk.
- **Investigator, not Judge:** the human-in-the-loop invariant is load-bearing across the whole design — no AI output ever changes a compliance verdict without a deterministic Control or a human.
- Storing customer financial evidence outside their ERP creates a data-residency/trust obligation that onboarding copy and the tenancy model must honor (ADR-0005, ADR-0007).
- Odoo→Process field mapping (which Odoo models map to PR/PO/GR/Bill/Payment activities), role/permission granularity (Admin/Auditor/Viewer), and 3-way-match edge cases (partial receipts, tolerances, multi-currency) are in-scope implementation details to be resolved during TDD, not separate design forks. Monetary fields are normalized to `Money` and evaluated per-currency (no cross-currency conversion in v1); see ADR-0011.

items.title: PostgreSQL connector: WARN spam from TypeRegistry in multi-schema deployments
items.body:
## Bug report

**What Debezium connector do you use and what version?**

`io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector`, version `3.4.3.Final` (also reproduced on `3.5.0.Final`)

---

**What is the connector configuration?**

```json
{
  "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
  "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
  "publication.autocreate.mode": "disabled",
  "publication.name": "cdc",
  "table.include.list": ".+\\.(table_a|table_b|table_c|table_d|...)$",
  "tasks.max": "1",
  "snapshot.mode": "no_data",
  "heartbeat.interval.ms": "5000"
}
```

Note: no `schema.include.list` — we capture from all tenant schemas by design.

---

**What is the captured database version and mode of deployment?**

Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, managed (AWS RDS), MSK Connect.

---

**What behavior do you expect?**

The "Type is already mapped" condition should not log at WARN level when the duplicate is simply a same-named type in a different schema. This is expected in any multi-tenant or multi-schema PostgreSQL deployment and is not indicative of a problem.

---

**What behavior do you see?**

~17,000 WARN-level log lines per connector startup:

```
WARN  Type [oid:278431, name:accounts] is already mapped   [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
WARN  Type [oid:278432, name:users] is already mapped       [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
WARN  Type [oid:278433, name:enrollments] is already mapped [io.debezium.connector.postgresql.TypeRegistry]
... (repeated for every type × every tenant schema)
```

On MSK Connect, there is no per-class log level configuration, so we cannot suppress these via logging config. The volume drowns out genuine warnings from the connector.

---

**Do you see the same behaviour using the latest released Debezium version?**

Yes — the `addType()` method is unchanged in `3.5.0.Final`. Not verified against any Alpha/Beta/CR builds, but the code path has not changed on `main`.

---

**Do you have the connector logs, ideally from start till finish?**

The relevant logs are the WARN lines themselves — samples are shown above.

---

**How to reproduce the issue using our [[tutorial](https://github.com/debezium/debezium-examples/tree/main/tutorial)](https://github.com/debezium/debezium-examples/tree/main/tutorial) deployment?**

1. Create a PostgreSQL database with multiple schemas sharing the same table definitions:

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_1;
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_2;
CREATE SCHEMA tenant_3;
-- repeat for N schemas

CREATE TABLE tenant_1.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
CREATE TABLE tenant_2.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
CREATE TABLE tenant_3.table_a (id bigint primary key, name text);
-- repeat for each schema
```

2. Configure the connector with `table.include.list` matching all schemas (no `schema.include.list`):

```json
{
  "table.include.list": ".+\\.table_a$"
}
```

3. Start the connector. Observe WARN lines for every `table_a` composite type after the first schema.

The number of warnings scales as `(num_schemas - 1) × num_types_per_schema`.

---

### Cause

In [`[TypeRegistry.addType()](https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/v3.5.0.Final/debezium-connector-postgres/src/main/java/io/debezium/connector/postgresql/TypeRegistry.java#L143-L147)`](https://github.com/debezium/debezium/blob/v3.5.0.Final/debezium-connector-postgres/src/main/java/io/debezium/connector/postgresql/TypeRegistry.java#L143-L147), the `nameToType` map is keyed solely by type name:

```java
if (!nameToType.containsKey(type.getName())) {
    nameToType.put(type.getName(), type);
}
else {
    LOGGER.warn("Type [oid:{}, name:{}] is already mapped", type.getOid(), type.getName());
}
```

The underlying `SQL_TYPES` query joins `pg_namespace` but the namespace is never propagated into the map key. When schema `tenant_1` and schema `tenant_2` both define a composite type `accounts`, the second one triggers a WARN.

In our environment (Canvas LMS — a multi-tenant PostgreSQL application), a single database has hundreds of schemas sharing identical table/type definitions. This produces **~17,000 WARN lines per connector startup**, repeated on every restart or rebalance.

### Why existing fixes don't help

- **PR #7150 (schema-filtered type loading)**: Filters `pg_type` to `schema.include.list` schemas. Our connector captures tables from _all_ schemas (`table.include.list: ".+\\.(table_names...)$"`) — we have no `schema.include.list` because every tenant schema is needed. Even if we enumerated all schemas, the duplicates across them would still trigger warnings.
- **DBZ-5182 (ascending OID order)**: Addressed type _collisions_ from extension schemas overriding built-in types, but did not change the log level or namespace handling.
- **#1683 / #1800 (performance fixes)**: Reduced startup time from OID lookups and double initialization, but the WARN-level logging remains.

### Relationship to [DBZ-8519](https://github.com/debezium/dbz/issues/1323)

[DBZ-8519](https://github.com/debezium/dbz/issues/1323) reports the same symptom but from a different angle — the reporter has many schemas and expected `schema.include.list` to suppress the warnings. Our case is distinct: we intentionally capture all schemas, so schema filtering is not a viable workaround. The underlying code issue (name-only keying, WARN log level) is the same.

### Suggested fix

Downgrade the log level from `LOGGER.warn` to `LOGGER.debug` in `TypeRegistry.addType()`. The "already mapped" condition is a normal consequence of PostgreSQL's type system when multiple schemas define same-named types. It is not a correctness issue — the first-registered type wins, and `oidToType` still maps every OID correctly. The `nameToType` map is used for well-known type name lookups (e.g., `hstore`, `geometry`) that don't carry schema context, so the first-wins behavior is the right semantics here.

## Current context

**Current state:** GitHub records this issue as closed.

**Context:** Azure SQL change data capture (CDC) records row changes for Debezium, the connector that reads SQL Server changes into Kafka. Kafka is the event log used by the platform. This issue covers the self-hosted CI runner, database permissions, and the security boundary for the capture path. **Why it matters:** the runner and grants determine whether the container checks can exercise the same tenant onboarding and CDC path used by the platform.

**Outcome:** PRs #160, #161, and #163 merged on 2026-08-25. They delivered the runner foundation and tenant database grants. Follow-on issue #68 was implemented in merged PRs #183, #186, and #187: the onboarding and connector path now carry the SQL Server signaling-table behavior and a Kafka Connect Filter, a record transform that drops signaling-table rows from the business event stream, needed for incremental snapshots. Current `main` at `fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f` is not one consistent public contract. `docs/blueprint.md` and `docs/specs/11-infra-disposable.md` still contain Outbox-only and read-only wording, while `tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql` and `connect/connectors/connector-template.json` contain the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` CDC and Filter path. The documentation correction remains an explicit follow-on boundary.

**Repository evidence:** [PR #160](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/160), [PR #161](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/161), and [PR #163](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/163) (merged 2026-08-25); [PR #183](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/183), [PR #186](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/186), and [PR #187](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/pull/187) (merged 2026-08-27). The current source files are [tenant-onboarding.sql](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/tools/onboarding/tenant-onboarding.sql) and [connector-template.json](https://github.com/collaborationwithothers/cdc-platform-azure/blob/fb29eeb3160bbce0c42469560609d254aabc272f/connect/connectors/connector-template.json).

## Unknowns

The current code and public documentation disagree about whether SQL Server CDC includes `dbo.DebeziumSignal` and whether the connector has a write grant on that table. The repository does not claim live Azure snapshot behavior or production-scale proof here.

## Historical evidence

The original issue body is retained below unchanged. It preserves the original behavior, blockers, paths, verification method, acceptance checklist, scope boundaries, size forecast, dates, and links.

<details>
<summary>Original issue body</summary>

## Behavior

An onboarding runner reads the tenant manifest and applies, per tenant database: the tenant schema including the Outbox table with its TraceParent column and the DebeziumSignal watermarking table, CDC on `dbo.Outbox` only, Change Tracking on `dbo.WorkflowTask` only, `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` on the database, and the TenantInfo claim row. Running it twice changes nothing and throws nothing. This T-SQL is the canonical definition of the tenant schema for the whole repository.

## Blocked by

- #31 (D3)

## Paths

- `tools/onboarding/`
- `tests/Lexfield.TestSupport/`
- `tests/Lexfield.Onboarding.Tests/`

## Verification

Method: containers

Run the runner against a Testcontainers SQL Server. Assert tables exist, including `dbo.DebeziumSignal`; `sys.databases.is_cdc_enabled`; a capture instance on `dbo.Outbox` and none on `dbo.WorkflowTask`; `sys.change_tracking_tables` contains `WorkflowTask` and nothing else; `sys.databases.snapshot_isolation_state` is on; the `TenantInfo` row holds the expected tenantId. Then run the whole thing a second time and assert nothing changed and nothing threw, which is the actual idempotency claim.

## Acceptance checklist

- [ ] `dbo.Outbox` is created with the nullable `TraceParent` column
- [ ] `dbo.DebeziumSignal` is created per tenant database for incremental-snapshot watermarking
- [ ] CDC is enabled on `dbo.Outbox` and on no other table
- [ ] Change Tracking is enabled on `dbo.WorkflowTask` and on no other table
- [ ] `ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION` is enabled on each tenant database
- [ ] The grant of INSERT and SELECT on `dbo.DebeziumSignal` only, to the connector identity, is authored in the canonical onboarding T-SQL; business and CDC tables stay read-only. Its execution against a real Entra user is verified in the live user-creation ticket
- [ ] The `TenantInfo` row holds the tenantId from the manifest
- [ ] A second run of the whole runner changes nothing and throws nothing, asserted rather than argued
- [ ] TestSupport switched to execute the canonical onboarding scripts; provisional DDL deleted

## Out of scope

- `CREATE USER FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER` and the execution of its grants (including the `dbo.DebeziumSignal` grant), which need a real Entra-backed server and are a separate live ticket. The grant T-SQL is authored here as part of the canonical scripts; only its execution is out of scope
- Connector registration, which is the connect area
- Any change to the schema contract itself; this ticket implements the contract, it does not redesign it

## Size forecast

8 files, 420 lines
