items.title: Self-healing live↔local cross-validation system for AEAT data

milestone.title: 0.1.0 — Kent can feed his bank data in and trust the classification
milestone.description: Kent success moment: Kent imports three bank-CSV exports (BBVA, Wise EUR, Wise GBP) with one command; the tool persists them, classifies most automatically via rules, leaves a small review queue for him, and shows him a single 'pipeline status' dashboard with confidence scores per decision. Everything works WITHOUT live AEAT reads — no cert-auth dependency. T1->T6 pipeline functional end-to-end locally.

items.body:
## Goal

Build a robust, self-healing system that continuously cross-references data fetched live from the AEAT *Sede Electrónica* against the data schemas defined locally on the client side, detects divergence, and either heals the local schemas automatically or surfaces the divergence to a human for review.

This is the keystone integration issue. It depends on browser automation, certificate auth, the schema extractor, the storage layer, and the modelo + portal catalogues all being in place.

## Background

Once #6 (modelo enum), #7 (portal catalogue), #8 (cert auth), #9 (schema extraction), and #10 (storage) exist, we have the parts but not the loop. The loop is:

1. **Fetch live** — authenticated session against AEAT, scrape current modelo structure, current period definitions, current portal endpoints, and any live filing-state data the user is allowed to read.
2. **Validate incoming** — every payload coming off the wire must be parsed through a strict, typed schema (pydantic / dataclass + validator). Garbage in is rejected at the boundary, never silently coerced.
3. **Cross-reference local** — the validated incoming data is compared field-by-field against the locally-persisted schemas / catalogues / cached extractions.
4. **Diff + classify divergence** — additive (new casilla, new period), breaking (renamed/removed casilla, formula change), benign (cosmetic label tweaks), or suspicious (data we didn't expect to change).
5. **Heal or escalate** — additive and benign changes are auto-applied to the local store via a migration; breaking or suspicious changes raise a structured alert and create a review record. Nothing destructive happens without a human-approved migration.
6. **Audit** — every fetch, validation, diff, and heal action is recorded in the storage layer (#10) with full provenance.

## Scope — research phase

- Survey approaches for **runtime schema validation** of incoming data: pydantic (already in the stack), msgspec, attrs+cattrs, marshmallow. Pick one — pydantic is the default, but justify it.
- Survey approaches for **schema-vs-schema diffing**: deepdiff, dictdiffer, custom AST walker, JSON Schema diff tools. The diff has to be semantic (it understands "casilla 03 was renamed", not just "key 03 changed").
- Investigate self-healing patterns from related projects (drift detection in Terraform, schema migration tools in CDC pipelines, contract testing frameworks like Pact).
- Persist findings in `.vault/research/` with an ADR in `.vault/adr/`.

## Scope — scaffolding phase

- Define the orchestration entry point under `src/aeat/sync/` (or similar): a `LiveSyncRunner` class that composes the auth backend (#8), the portal catalogue (#7), the schema extractors (#9), and the storage layer (#10) into one coherent loop.
- Define the **typed wire schemas** that every incoming payload from AEAT is parsed through. These are *separate* from the persisted local schemas — wire schemas describe what AEAT actually serves; local schemas describe our canonical model. The cross-reference layer is what bridges them.
- Define the **divergence record** type stored in the storage layer: timestamp, source URL, modelo + period, classification (additive / breaking / benign / suspicious), structured diff payload, resolution state (pending / auto-healed / human-approved / rejected).
- Define the **healing strategies** as pluggable handlers keyed on classification, so new strategies can be added without rewriting the runner.
- A CLI entry point (e.g. `aeat sync run --modelo 130 --period 2026Q1 [--auto-heal]`) — actual scheduling is a follow-up.
- Settings additions in `src/aeat/config.py` (pydantic-settings) for: sync concurrency, auto-heal allowlist, divergence alert sink (file / email / webhook stub), retry policy. Documented in `env/.env.example` (per #4) and enforced by `tests/test_config.py`.

## Tests

- **Unit tests** (`@pytest.mark.unit`):
  - Each wire schema rejects malformed payloads with clear errors.
  - The diff classifier categorises every kind of divergence on synthetic fixtures.
  - Each healing strategy is exercised with synthetic divergence records.
  - The runner composes correctly when individual components are stubbed at the public-API boundary (no internal mocking, no patching of private state).
- **Live tests** (`@pytest.mark.live`, never using mocks/fakes/stubs/patches):
  - End-to-end fetch → validate → diff → record against a live AEAT pre-login or low-risk gated endpoint.
  - These are skipped by default and require a real certificate (#8) plus explicit opt-in via env var. Document the opt-in clearly.

## Out of scope

- Actually filing any modelo. This issue is read-only against AEAT.
- Multi-user / multi-client orchestration.
- A UI for reviewing divergence records — CLI listing only.
- Automatic remediation of *AEAT-side* issues (e.g. retrying their server errors). The healing here is local-schema healing only.
- Notifications beyond a structured log sink and the divergence-record table.

## Acceptance

- Vault research artifact + ADR for the validation, diffing, and healing approach.
- `src/aeat/sync/` scaffolded with the runner, wire schemas, divergence records, and pluggable healing strategies — all typed, docstring-ed, and unit-tested.
- CLI entry point wired through the existing entry-point pattern.
- Settings + `env/.env.example` updated and `tests/test_config.py` aligned.
- Live tests written, skipped by default, runnable via opt-in env var. Documented in the issue/ADR.
- A documented self-heal allowlist policy: which divergence classes are safe to auto-apply, which always escalate.

## Notes

This issue is deliberately ambitious. It is the place where every other foundational issue earns its keep — if any of #6, #7, #8, #9, #10 has the wrong shape, this is where it shows up. Expect to file follow-up issues against the foundations as the integration surfaces real friction.

The "self-healing" property is bounded: only **additive** and **explicitly allowlisted** changes ever auto-apply. Anything that could lose data, change semantics of existing casillas, or remove fields is **always** routed to human review. Bias toward safety; we are operating against a tax authority.

## Dependencies

- **Hard:** #6 (modelo enum), #7 (portal catalogue), #8 (certificate auth), #9 (schema extraction), #10 (storage). All five must land in at least scaffold form before this issue's scaffolding phase can compile, and in at least proof-of-concept form before the live tests can run.
- **Soft:** #4 (dev scaffolding) for the CLI / justfile / env wiring.

items.title: RFC: Provider-keyed `detection:` config (ADR-033.1)
items.body:
## Summary

Extend `DetectionConfig` (#226-1) and the per-entity codegen factory (#226-7) to support **multiple providers per entity** as the default shape. Today's schema and template assume one entity = one source; the dogfood consumer (dealbrain-v2) and the canonical CRM-sync use case both sync each entity from multiple providers (HubSpot + Salesforce) simultaneously. This was deferred from the original epic, not designed against — proposing **ADR-033.1** to lock the extension.

Reference consumer: [pattern-stack/sales-patterns-ts#60](https://github.com/pattern-stack/sales-patterns-ts/pull/60) — six tuples (3 entities × 2 providers) hand-authored against #226-7's runtime primitives, demonstrating the shape this RFC formalizes.

This RFC has **two parts**. Part 1 is the core change; Part 2 is an isolated optional artifact emission that can ship in parallel and on its own.

---

## Part 1 — Provider-keyed `detection:` (core)

### Schema delta

Single shape, always provider-keyed. No scalar back-compat (the dogfood consumer is the only caller; back-compat shims earn nothing here):

```ts
// src/schema/entity-definition.schema.ts
detection: z.record(z.string(), DetectionConfigSchema).optional(),
```

The inner `DetectionConfigSchema` (`runtime/subsystems/sync/detection-config.schema.ts`) is **untouched** — it still discriminates on `mode: 'poll' | 'webhook'` with the same `cursor`, `mapping[]`, `filters[]` fields. Provider identity becomes structure (the YAML key), not a new schema field. Each provider's block is an independent `DetectionConfig`.

```yaml
# entities/opportunity.yaml
detection:
  hubspot-crm:
    mode: poll
    poll: { cursor: { kind: 'timestamp', field: 'hs_lastmodifieddate' } }
    mapping:
      - { source: id,            target: external_id }
      - { source: dealname,      target: name }
      - { source: hubspot_owner_id, target: owner_external_id }
    filters:
      - { field: archived, op: eq, value: false }
  salesforce-crm:
    mode: poll
    poll: { cursor: { kind: 'systemModstamp', field: 'SystemModstamp' } }
    mapping:
      - { source: Id,      target: external_id }
      - { source: Name,    target: name }
      - { source: OwnerId, target: owner_external_id }
    filters:
      - { field: IsDeleted, op: eq, value: false }
```

### Codegen template

One generated module **per entity** — *not* per `(entity, provider)` tuple. The generated file contains **no provider-specific symbols, no provider-specific branching, no per-provider class imports**. Provider strings appear only as map keys lifted from YAML (data, not logic). All per-provider variation flows through DI tokens the consumer fills.

```ts
// generated: src/modules/.../<entity>-sync-source.module.ts
const OPPORTUNITY_DETECTION_CONFIGS: Record<string, DetectionConfig> = {
  'hubspot-crm':    { mode: 'poll', poll: { cursor: { kind: 'timestamp',      field: 'hs_lastmodifieddate' } }, mapping: [...], filters: [...] },
  'salesforce-crm': { mode: 'poll', poll: { cursor: { kind: 'systemModstamp', field: 'SystemModstamp'      } }, mapping: [...], filters: [...] },
};

export const OPPORTUNITY_POLL_FETCH_REGISTRY = Symbol('OPPORTUNITY_POLL_FETCH_REGISTRY');
export const OPPORTUNITY_CHANGE_SOURCES      = Symbol('OPPORTUNITY_CHANGE_SOURCES');

@Module({
  providers: [
    {
      provide: OPPORTUNITY_CHANGE_SOURCES,
      inject:  [OPPORTUNITY_POLL_FETCH_REGISTRY /*, middleware tokens */],
      useFactory: (fetches: Record<string, PollFetchCallback<Opportunity>>) =>
        new Map(
          Object.entries(OPPORTUNITY_DETECTION_CONFIGS).map(([provider, cfg]) =>
            [provider, buildChangeSource(cfg, fetches[provider] /*, middlewares */)],
          ),
        ),
    },
  ],
  exports: [OPPORTUNITY_CHANGE_SOURCES],
})
export class OpportunitySyncSourceModule {}
```

`prompt.js` change: detect `definition.detection` (always object, always keyed); iterate `Object.entries()` to emit the configs map. No `isMultiProvider` branch needed since single-provider is the same loop with a one-key map.

**Drop the `isCleanArchitecture` gate.** `templates/entity/new/backend/modules/core/sync-source.ejs.t` currently has:
```
skip_if: <%= !hasDetection || !isCleanArchitecture %>
```
The architecture predicate is wrong here — sync-source modules belong wherever modules are emitted (`clean-lite-ps` included). Fix:
```
skip_if: <%= !hasDetection %>
```
This is part of the RFC's scope; not a separate PR (the file doesn't exist on `main` until #240 lands).

### Token naming

No `<PROVIDER>_<ENTITY>_*` symbols. Provider names live exclusively as runtime map keys. Generated tokens are entity-level only:
- `<ENTITY>_DETECTION_CONFIGS` (literal, internal to the module)
- `<ENTITY>_POLL_FETCH_REGISTRY` (consumer fills)
- `<ENTITY>_CHANGE_SOURCES` (factory output, consumer reads)

### Pre-emission YAML validation

`pts codegen entity validate` adds a refinement: every key under `detection:` must also exist under that entity's `sync.providers:`. Catches typos (`hubspot-cmr`) and forgotten registrations at validate-time, not at runtime.

```ts
EntityDefinitionSchema.superRefine((entity, ctx) => {
  if (!entity.detection) return;
  const declared = new Set(Object.keys(entity.sync?.providers ?? {}));
  for (const provider of Object.keys(entity.detection)) {
    if (!declared.has(provider)) {
      ctx.addIssue({
        code: 'custom',
        path: ['detection', provider],
        message: `Provider '${provider}' used in detection: but not declared in sync.providers. Known providers: ${[...declared].join(', ')}`,
      });
    }
  }
});
```

### Mixed mode per provider

Supported by construction. Each provider's value is an independent `DetectionConfig`; one entity can declare HubSpot as `mode: webhook` while Salesforce stays `mode: poll`. A `sync_subscription` is `(integration, entity)` — so HubSpot's webhook subscription and Salesforce's poll subscription are already two orchestrator runs. No orchestrator change. The factory's `buildChangeSource` switches on `cfg.mode` to instantiate `PollChangeSource<T>` or `WebhookChangeSource<T>`.

### Filters — per-provider only, no inheritance

Each provider's `filters[]` is independent. No entity-level filters, no merging, no overriding. If two providers happen to share a filter, copy-paste or YAML anchors (`&defaults` / `<<: *defaults`). Inheritance is the kind of feature that's nice for two days then confusing forever.

### Cursor disambiguation

`sync_subscriptions.cursor` stays opaque. The subscription row's `provider` column already disambiguates which YAML detection block parses the cursor — no need to tag the cursor itself with `kind`. Provider key is the indirection.

### Storage uniqueness — consumer-side, not RFC scope

Worth flagging since multi-provider per entity is the trigger: consumers must use a composite unique constraint on synced entity tables (`user_id`, `provider`, `external_id`) to prevent collisions when two providers happen to share an external_id. The `external_id_tracking` behavior already gives entities a `provider` column; only the unique-key declaration needs to include it. Filed separately on the dogfood side; not part of the codegen-patterns change.

### ADR

Lock as **ADR-033.1** (extension), not amend ADR-033 in place. Original ADR-033's locked decisions stand; provider-keying is a follow-on the audit trail can read independently.

---

## Part 2 — Typed provider artifacts (optional, parallelizable)

**This sub-section can ship independently of Part 1 and on its own timeline.** Either order is valid; merging Part 2 alone gives consumers type safety even when they hand-author the modules; merging Part 1 alone gives the core feature with weaker consumer type checking. They share an entity-YAML pass but not an emission path.

### What it emits

Alongside `<entity>-sync-source.module.ts`, emit a small TS file:

```ts
// generated: src/modules/.../<entity>-sync-source.providers.ts
export const OPPORTUNITY_PROVIDERS = ['hubspot-crm', 'salesforce-crm'] as const;
export type OpportunityProvider = (typeof OPPORTUNITY_PROVIDERS)[number];
```

### Why

Consumer registry maps and DI tokens become typed:

```ts
useFactory: (hs, sfdc): Record<OpportunityProvider, PollFetchCallback<Opportunity>> => ({
  'hubspot-crm':    hs.opportunityPollFetch,
  'salesforce-crm': sfdc.opportunityPollFetch,
});
```

Typo (`'hubspot-cmr'`), missing provider, or stale registry after YAML change → TS compile error. dbt-style: YAML is the source of truth, codegen emits typed artifacts, consumer is checked against them.

### Properties

- One file per entity that has a `detection:` block.
- Zero runtime cost (literal-tuple type only).
- No coupling to Part 1's emission path — independent template.
- Trivially regenerated.

### Acceptance

- `bun run typecheck` of the consumer rejects a typo (`'hubspot-cmr'`) in the registry.
- Adding a provider to YAML and re-running codegen breaks consumer typecheck on incomplete registry maps until the consumer updates.

---

## Out of scope

- **Filter vocabulary expansion** (OR / NOT / nested predicates) — deferred upstream per epic open Q3.
- **CDC streaming primitive** (#226-8) — separate runtime primitive, not affected.
- **Webhook factory codegen emission** — Phase 2 emits poll-only; webhook factory follows when first consumer demands.
- **`subscription.config` per-provider runtime overlays** — separate concern (Q3 deferred).
- **Mode fallback semantics** (CDC drops → poll resumes) — epic open Q2.
- **Inbound webhook staging-table schema** — consumer-owned per ADR-002 §Phase 4.
- **Cross-tenant provider registry / dynamic provider plugins** — explicit YAML keys only.

## Open questions for review

1. Should provider-name validation (Part 1's `superRefine`) also cross-check against a project-level `codegen.config.yaml` registry of known providers? Within-file consistency catches the practical typo class; project-level adds strictness with more wiring. Recommend within-file only for v1.
2. Is `Record<string, DetectionConfig>` the right Zod shape, or should provider keys be a project-level enum? Enum gives stronger typing but couples entity YAML to project config. Recommend `z.record` for v1; tighten later if needed.
3. Token export naming: `<ENTITY>_CHANGE_SOURCES` (plural Map) vs splitting into `<ENTITY>_HUBSPOT_CHANGE_SOURCE` / etc. (which contradicts the no-provider-symbols decision). Recommend Map.
4. For the optional Part 2: filename — `<entity>-sync-source.providers.ts` or fold into the existing module file as additional exports? Separate file is cleaner for codegen but adds an artifact. Recommend separate.

## Reference consumer

[pattern-stack/sales-patterns-ts#60](https://github.com/pattern-stack/sales-patterns-ts/pull/60) hand-authored the six target tuples (3 entities × 2 providers) against #226-1's `PollChangeSource<T>` + `createLoopbackMiddleware`. Reading those modules gives the exact shape this RFC's codegen output should match. The hand-authored modules will be deleted in a follow-up issue once codegen lands.

items.title: research: Lakehouse backing store deep dive — BigQuery
items.body:
**Parent: #15 — Production lakehouse adapter (BigQuery / ClickHouse Cloud)**

One of three deep-research sub-issues spawned from #15. Sister to the **ClickHouse Cloud** deep-dive sub-issue; structure your output so the two are directly comparable. Architecture-level decisions (where the lakehouse lives, who writes to it) are tracked in the **architecture / ingestion-contract** sub-issue, but this research should sketch schemas and access patterns concretely in parallel.

## Goal

Produce a research packet that, taken together with the ClickHouse Cloud counterpart, lets us pick a backing store with confidence and start implementation.

## Context

### Existing surface (recap from parent)

- `types/lakehouse.go::TraceLakehouse` — five-method interface backing today's CLI subcommands (`baseline`, `mine-failures`, `drift`, `compare-to-production`).
- `types/runtrace.go::RunTrace`, `RunRecording`, `ToolCallSummary`, `VerificationResult`.
- `types/metrics.go::TraceFilter`, `TraceMetrics`, `BaselineMetrics`, `DriftReport`.
- `eval/lakehouse/filestore.go` — the contract reference implementation. Note `parentOnlyToolCalls` (`filestore.go:239`) — sub-agent calls forwarded into the parent trace must be excluded from per-run aggregates (#55).
- `eval/cmd/eval/main.go` — the only consumer today.

### Read patterns the lakehouse must serve well

These come from `eval/cmd/eval/main.go` and the `TraceLakehouse` interface:

- **`Metrics(filter)`** — count, pass rate, mean turns, mean tokens, p50/p95 wall-clock duration over a window, optionally filtered by mode/model/outcome. Used by `baseline`, `drift`, and `compare-to-production`.
- **`QueryTraces(filter)` ordered by `StartedAt desc` with limit** — used to render recent runs and feed CI comparisons.
- **`QueryRecordings(filter)`** — only used by `mine-failures` today. Recordings carry full transcripts; this query touches a much heavier table.
- **Future: drift over arbitrary windows / cohort comparison.** `cmdDrift` does this now over two adjacent windows; we'll want richer slice-and-dice.

### Write patterns

- **`StoreTrace`** — one event per run completion, low-rate at first (10s–100s/day in early CP deployments), scaling toward 10k+/day as the agent product matures. Bursty (CI gate runs).
- **`StoreRecording`** — same per-run rate, but each payload is large (typical run: 5–20 turns, model input + output per turn, tool I/O captured verbatim). Easily megabytes.

### Constraints

- Cost-conscious early-stage deployment. Don't wake up to a four-figure monthly bill from streaming inserts + scan-heavy queries.
- Retain raw recordings for at least 30 days (mining failures, debugging incidents); aggregate trace metrics indefinitely.
- Schema evolution will happen. `RunTrace` already grew `RunID`/`ParentRunID` (#55).
- Compliance posture (#8): recordings are confidential by default; column-level / row-level access policy support is a plus.

## Research questions

1. **Schema design.** What's the right shape for `RunTrace` in BigQuery — fully-flattened columns, mostly columns plus a `JSON` blob for evolving fields, or a single `JSON` column per row? How do we handle nested arrays (`ToolCalls`, `VerificationResults`) — `REPEATED RECORD`, `ARRAY<STRUCT<…>>`, or `JSON`? Specifically address the `parentOnlyToolCalls` filter — it must be cheap as a predicate.
2. **`RunRecording` storage.** Three live options: (a) wide BigQuery table with the recording as a `JSON`/`STRING` column, (b) BigQuery row pointing to a GCS object holding the recording JSON, (c) BigQuery EXTERNAL or BigLake table over GCS. Which optimises scan cost / mining query latency / retention controls? How does the choice interact with #8's RunRecording-encryption requirement?
3. **Partitioning & clustering.** What partition keys (ingestion-time vs `started_at` vs `completed_at`) and clustering keys (`outcome`, `mode`, `model`, `tenant_id`) minimise scan bytes for our specific queries? Provide concrete recommendations rather than generic advice.
4. **Ingestion mechanism.** Streaming inserts (`tabledata.insertAll`) vs Storage Write API (recommended for Go; supports CDC, exactly-once, lower per-row cost) vs batch loads from GCS. What's the recommended pattern for control-plane-driven writes from Go (`cloud.google.com/go/bigquery/storage/managedwriter`)? Latency, cost-per-million-rows, retry/idempotency story.
5. **Cost model.** Estimated monthly cost at 10k runs/day and 100k runs/day. Storage (active vs long-term partitions), ingestion (Storage Write API vs streaming legacy), query (on-demand $/TiB-scanned vs slot-based reservations). Where do the cliffs and footguns sit (e.g. `SELECT *` over a JSON column scanning the whole row group)?
6. **Query ergonomics.** Translate the current `Metrics` helper (`computeMetrics` in `filestore.go`) into a representative BigQuery query. How much does `APPROX_QUANTILES` save on p50/p95? Materialized views for the common drift queries — useful or premature?
7. **Schema evolution.** What's BigQuery's behaviour when adding a column to a `STRUCT` inside a nested array? Versus a `JSON` typed column? What's the operational cost of the migration path we'd actually use, walked through against a concrete upcoming change (e.g. multimodal `ContentBlock` variants from #103)?
8. **PII / secret scrubbing & access control.** Column-level access (`policy_tags`, dynamic data masking) vs row-level access policies vs separate datasets per classification. What does enforcing the #8 RunRecording encryption requirement (AES-256-GCM keyed from `SecretStore`) look like — CMEK, app-level, or both?
9. **Multi-tenancy.** Per-tenant dataset, per-tenant project, or `tenant_id` column with row-level access policy? What scales to 100 tenants? 10k? What does the read API surface look like at each tier?
10. **Open-table interop.** BigLake / Iceberg-on-GCS — useful for "we can swap engines later", or operational dead weight at our scale?
11. **Observability of the lakehouse itself.** `INFORMATION_SCHEMA` tables, Cloud Logging, Cloud Monitoring metrics — what does an SRE looking at "is ingestion stuck?" actually look at? Slot utilisation alarms? What's the dead-letter pattern for failed inserts?
12. **Go client maturity.** `cloud.google.com/go/bigquery` and the `managedwriter` package — known sharp edges, dependency surface, auth flows for control plane (Workload Identity vs service account JSON), test ergonomics (emulator vs sandbox project).

## Deliverables

A research packet covering:

- **Recommended schema** (DDL sketches for `traces` and `recordings` tables) with partitioning + clustering keys justified against the query workload.
- **Recommended ingestion path** with sample Go code outline (Storage Write API or streaming legacy), retry / idempotency policy, and observability hooks.
- **Cost model** at the two scale points above with the math shown (and your assumptions).
- **Query rewrites** for the four `eval` subcommands (`baseline`, `mine-failures`, `drift`, `compare-to-production`) — actual SQL, not pseudocode.
- **Schema-evolution recipe** that walks through a likely upcoming change (e.g. multimodal `ContentBlock` variants from #103).
- **Security posture** for the #8 encryption + classification requirements: which BigQuery feature satisfies which line-item.
- **Multi-tenancy recommendation** with a clear "small fleet" → "fleet at 10k tenants" growth path.
- **Operational runbook outline:** alerts, dashboards, dead-letter handling for failed inserts, "ingestion is stuck" playbook.
- **Comparative honesty:** where would BigQuery be a *worse* fit than ClickHouse Cloud? Open the door for the sister sub-issue to call those out.

## Inputs the researcher should pull from

- **In-tree code:** `types/lakehouse.go`, `types/runtrace.go`, `types/metrics.go`, `eval/lakehouse/filestore.go` (mirror the contract exactly), `eval/cmd/eval/main.go` (see actual query callers).
- **Related issues:** #8 (RunRecording encryption / classification / RBAC), #9 (eval mining quarantine), #13 (mine first eval suite), #15 (parent), #55 (sub-agent forwarding), #103 (multimodal — drives recording size). The OTel exporter context from #100 is relevant for understanding the wire format the control plane would consume.
- **External primary sources:** BigQuery Storage Write API docs, BigQuery `JSON` column docs, partitioning / clustering best practices, BigQuery pricing (active vs long-term storage, on-demand vs reservations), `cloud.google.com/go/bigquery` reference, BigLake / Iceberg announcements, GCP architecture-centre articles for "audit logs in BigQuery"-style workloads (closest analogue), recent re:Invent / Google Cloud Next talks on agent / LLM analytics on BigQuery.
- **Cross-reference:** at least one public agent-platform write-up that names BigQuery as their store, or a "we tried BigQuery and switched" post — both are useful signal.

## Out of scope

- The architecture / ownership question (covered in the sister architecture sub-issue).
- The ClickHouse Cloud analysis (covered in the sister CH Cloud sub-issue).
- Implementation work — this is research only.

items.title: [FEATURE] Add Encina.Audit.Marten — event-sourced IAuditStore with temporal crypto-shredding for compliance-grade audit trails

labels.name: area-compliance
labels.description: GDPR, EU Laws, and Regulatory Compliance patterns

milestone.title: Post-1.0: Security Core Completion (deferred items)
milestone.description: Security core: Core abstractions, ABAC, PII masking, field-level encryption, audit trail, anti-tampering, sanitization, secrets management (ISecretProvider + 4 cloud providers), XACML policy serialization, persistent PAP, and Attestation framework.

items.body:
## Feature Description
Add `Encina.Audit.Marten` as an **additional provider** for `IAuditStore` and `IReadAuditStore`, implementing event-sourced audit trails with temporal crypto-shredding via Marten (PostgreSQL).
This follows the Encina "pay-for-what-you-use" philosophy:
- **Simple apps** ÔÇö `InMemoryAuditStore` (dev) or DB provider (production)
- **Compliance-heavy apps** (SOX, NIS2) ÔÇö `MartenAuditStore` with immutable events + crypto-shredding
The existing `IAuditStore` interface does NOT change ÔÇö this is a new implementation, not a migration.
## Motivation
- **SOX 404**: Requires immutable audit trail of internal controls. Current mutable stores allow tampering.
- **NIS2 Art. 10**: Requires logging with integrity guarantees. Append-only event store provides this.
- **GDPR Art. 5(1)(e)**: Data minimization requires purging old audit data. Crypto-shredding achieves this without breaking immutability.
- **Forensics**: Temporal queries ("what happened at time X?") are natural with event sourcing.
## Design (Option C from architectural review)
```
IAuditStore (unchanged interface)
|-- InMemoryAuditStore          ÔÇö development/testing (existing)
|-- DB providers (13)           ÔÇö production simple (existing)
+-- MartenAuditStore (NEW)      ÔÇö production compliance-grade
    |-- Events encrypted with temporal keys (monthly/yearly)
    |-- PurgeEntriesAsync() destroys temporal keys (crypto-shredding)
    |-- Marten projections for efficient querying
    +-- ITemporalKeyProvider for key lifecycle management
```
### Key Behaviors
| Operation | DB Provider (current) | MartenAuditStore (new) |
|-----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `RecordAsync` | INSERT row | Append encrypted event |
| `QueryAsync` | SELECT with filters | Project from decrypted events |
| `PurgeEntriesAsync` | DELETE rows | Destroy temporal encryption keys |
| Immutability | Rows can be UPDATE/DELETE'd | Events are append-only |
| Tamper evidence | None | Event stream integrity |
### Configuration
```csharp
// Simple app ÔÇö existing DB provider (no change)
services.AddEncinaAudit(options => { ... });
// Compliance-grade ÔÇö opt-in to Marten ES provider
services.AddEncinaAuditMarten(options =>
{
    options.KeyRotationPeriod = TimeSpan.FromDays(365); // yearly keys
    options.EncryptionScope = AuditEncryptionScope.PiiFieldsOnly;
    options.RetentionPeriod = TimeSpan.FromDays(2555); // 7 years (SOX)
    options.EnableAutoPurge = true;
});
```
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `MartenAuditStore` implements `IAuditStore` with event-sourced persistence
- [ ] `MartenReadAuditStore` implements `IReadAuditStore` with event-sourced persistence
- [ ] Audit events are encrypted with temporal keys via `ITemporalKeyProvider`
- [ ] `PurgeEntriesAsync()` destroys temporal keys (crypto-shredding), does NOT delete events
- [ ] Marten projections enable efficient `QueryAsync` with filtering and pagination
- [ ] Shredded entries are handled gracefully in query results (placeholder or skip)
- [ ] `ServiceCollectionExtensions.AddEncinaAuditMarten()` registers all components
- [ ] Existing `IAuditStore` implementations are NOT affected
- [ ] Unit tests with mocked `IAggregateRepository<T>`
- [ ] Integration tests against real Marten/PostgreSQL (Docker)
## Cross-Cutting Integration Checklist
- [x] OpenTelemetry ÔÇö inherit from Security.Audit diagnostics
- [x] Structured Logging ÔÇö inherit from Security.Audit logging
- [x] Health Checks ÔÇö verify Marten/PostgreSQL connectivity
- [x] Audit Trail ÔÇö this IS the audit trail implementation
- [ ] Caching ÔÇö evaluate caching projections for read-heavy queries
- N/A: Validation, Resilience (local DB), Distributed Locks, Transactions (Marten session), Idempotency (event versioning), Module Isolation
- Deferred: Multi-Tenancy (#798)
## Dependencies
- **Blocked by**: SPIKE issue for temporal crypto-shredding design (must be completed first)
- **Depends on**: #395 (Audit Trail Logging) ÔÇö `IAuditStore` interface
- **Depends on**: Encina.Marten.GDPR ÔÇö crypto-shredding reference pattern
- **Related**: #797 (Security module testing) ÔÇö integration tests for this provider
## Package Structure
```
src/
+-- Encina.Audit.Marten/
    |-- MartenAuditStore.cs           ÔÇö IAuditStore implementation
    |-- MartenReadAuditStore.cs       ÔÇö IReadAuditStore implementation
    |-- Events/
    |   |-- AuditEntryRecorded.cs     ÔÇö ES event
    |   +-- ReadAuditEntryRecorded.cs ÔÇö ES event
    |-- Projections/
    |   |-- AuditEntryProjection.cs   ÔÇö Read model for queries
    |   +-- ReadAuditProjection.cs    ÔÇö Read model for read audit
    |-- Crypto/
    |   |-- ITemporalKeyProvider.cs   ÔÇö Temporal key lifecycle
    |   +-- TemporalKeyProvider.cs    ÔÇö Marten-backed implementation
    |-- ServiceCollectionExtensions.cs
    |-- MartenAuditOptions.cs
    +-- Diagnostics/
        +-- MartenAuditDiagnostics.cs
```

items.title: CDC Debezium Connector isn't allowing to specify replication slot name

labels.name: type/bug
labels.description: The PR fixed a bug or issue reported a bug

items.body:
I think that it's safe to say that Apache Pulsar has multi-tenancy as a first-class citizen. However, when using it with CDC PostgreSQL Debezium Connector we actually have a issue that isn't allowing to separate data from different tenants.

Most companies use a schema-per-tenant approach when it comes to multi-tenancy so it is desirable to have a source connector for each schema. However, when using a standard configuration for PostgreSQL CDC Source Connector it creates a replication slot with the name "debezium" on PostgreSQL database. If we try to specify "slot.name" property it simply replies with "IO Exception". 

**It would be desirable to allow to specify the pg_replication_slot's name (possibly with the tenant's name) and this could be fixed by allowing to use Debezium's "slot.name" property.**
